title: Joint species distribution modelling for restoration of American chestnut (Castanea dentata) in the United States under current and future climate conditions
content:
Our joint species distribution modelling approach highlights its value in guiding the adaptive restoration of functionally extinct species in forests shaped by past and ongoing disturbance. We predicted a northward shift in species associated with American chestnut and identified lands already set aside for conservation where conditions are likely to be suitable for its long-term survival under climate change. These results provide actionable guidance for expanding experimental assisted migration and restoration plantings of blight-resistant American chestnut throughout and beyond its historical range.


Abstract

American chestnut (Castanea dentata) was once a dominant tree species spanning the eastern temperate forests of the United States until the introduction of chestnut blight in the early twentieth century resulted in its functional extinction. Recent advances in the development of blight-resistant American chestnut could support widespread restoration, but optimal locations for restoration plantings remain uncertain. Previous models of American chestnut created to address this question rely on post-blight occurrence data and pseudo-absences which likely underrepresent its distribution. They also omit abundance information, which may be critical for identifying successful restoration sites. Additionally, climate change is shifting the locations of suitable habitat for eastern temperate trees like American chestnut, complicating long-term restoration planning. We use a Bayesian joint species distribution modelling (JSDM) framework to jointly model current and future suitability for 11 chestnut-associated tree species within a broader assemblage of 39 tree species commonly found in eastern temperate forests. We identified a poleward shift in habitat for the forest communities American chestnut historically occurred with. Especially suitable areas were in the northeastern United States and northern Michigan, as well as possible refugia in higher elevation areas of the Appalachian Mountains. These areas overlap with 2988 existing conservation properties most suitable for restoration. Synthesis and applications. Our joint species distribution modelling approach highlights its value in guiding the adaptive restoration of functionally extinct species in forests shaped by past and ongoing disturbance. We predicted a northward shift in species associated with American chestnut and identified lands already set aside for conservation where conditions are likely to be suitable for its long-term survival under climate change. These results provide actionable guidance for expanding experimental assisted migration and restoration plantings of blight-resistant American chestnut throughout and beyond its historical range.
